working_title: Did a Baker Really Burn Down London?
hook: Everyone knows the Great Fire of London started in a bakery, but what really happened?

scenes.narration: The Great Fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane on September second, 1666.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a narrow medieval London lane at night, warm ochre and brick red palette, visible paper grain, gentle glow from a small bakery window, soft rim light, calm composition, vertical 9:16.

scenes.narration: It began past midnight on Pudding Lane as embers caught fuel.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a cozy dark bakery interior with glowing orange embers on a stone hearth, warm brick red and ochre tones, visible paper grain, soft rim light, calm composition, vertical 9:16 framing.

scenes.narration: Popular myth says the city was unprepared, but reality is more complex.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of crowded timber houses with overhanging upper stories almost touching across an alley, teal shadows and warm ochre walls, soft depth haze, vertical 9:16.

scenes.narration: Historians note London was a wooden maze of houses with narrow streets.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of distant wooden gables and slate roofs under a warm twilight sky, visible paper grain, soft muted palette, vertical 9:16.

scenes.narration: When flames began, the Lord Mayor hesitated to order necessary demolitions.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a worried official in period dress looking at a small flickering spark near timber beams, warm ochre tones, simple silhouettes, vertical 9:16.

scenes.narration: Fearing rebellion, officials also initially refused royal troops and help.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of empty medieval cobblestone streets at dusk, dark brick red and deep teal tones, quiet atmosphere, vertical 9:16.

scenes.narration: Instead of spreading unchecked, the fire stopped due to two key factors.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a distant stone tower silhouette against a calming sky, soft golden rim light, paper texture, vertical 9:16.

scenes.narration: The strong east wind dropped, and the garrison used gunpowder for firebreaks.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a tiny puff of smoke near a sturdy stone fortress wall, ochre and deep brick red palette, calm composition, vertical 9:16.

scenes.narration: While landmarks fell, London rose again on its familiar street plan.
scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a classic stone monument column topped with a glowing golden urn under a soft warm sky, visible paper grain, vertical 9:16.

scenes.visual: Hand-painted gouache storybook illustration of a quiet London street at dawn, warm ochre buildings, gentle depth haze, cozy and peaceful atmosphere, vertical 9:16.

why_it_matters: Distinguishes popular myth from historical evidence regarding the Great Fire of London.
structure: Myth versus fact: state the popular version, then carefully show what the evidence actually says.

claims.claim: The Great Fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane on September second, 1666.
Popular myth says the city was unprepared, but reality is more complex.
Historians note London was a wooden maze of houses with narrow streets.
When flames began, the Lord Mayor hesitated to order necessary demolitions.
Fearing rebellion, officials also initially refused royal troops and help.
Instead of spreading unchecked, the fire stopped due to two key factors.
The strong east wind dropped, and the garrison used gunpowder for firebreaks.
While landmarks fell, London rose again on its familiar street plan.
